gloss_terse: Ammishaddai — a Danite leader whose name means 'my kinsman is Shaddai'
gloss_readable: Ammishaddai is the father of Ahiezer, chieftain of the tribe of Dan during the wilderness period. The name is a theophoric compound combining 'ammi' (my kinsman) with 'Shaddai' (the Almighty), expressing a confession that God is as close as family. He appears exclusively in Numbers in census, camp arrangement, and offering contexts (Num 1:12; 7:66–71; 10:25). The LXX renders it Αμ(ε)ισαδαι, preserving both elements of the name.

senses.1: Personal name of the Danite leader, father of Ahiezer, appearing only in Numbers during the wilderness census and tribal offering narratives. The theophoric name declares divine kinship: 'my people-group is Shaddai.' Spanish 'Amisadai' and English 'Ammishaddai' both transliterate the compound faithfully, attesting its stable transmission across versions.

gloss_terse: toiling, laboring — one who works with wearisome effort (Ecclesiastes only)
gloss_readable: A verbal adjective used exclusively in Ecclesiastes to describe the person engaged in toilsome labor. Qoheleth uses it to probe the futility of human exertion: what does the toiler gain from all his striving (Eccl 3:9)? The word carries a note of weariness absent from neutral work-terms. Spanish 'trabaja' (he labors) and French 'labeur' (toil) both capture the exhausting quality, while German 'Muehe' (effort, trouble) highlights the burden side of the semantic range.

senses.1: Describes the person who toils with wearisome, burdensome labor — used predicatively in Ecclesiastes to characterize human striving under the sun. In Eccl 2:18 and 9:9, the toiler confronts the irony that his labor's fruit passes to another. The multilingual evidence converges: Spanish 'trabaja,' French 'labeur,' and German 'Muehe' all stress effortful exertion rather than simple activity.

gloss_terse: Amasai — name of several Israelites: a warrior of David, Levites, and a priest
gloss_readable: Amasai is the name borne by at least four distinct individuals in the Hebrew Bible. The most notable is the warrior who declared allegiance to David with a Spirit-inspired speech (1 Chr 12:19), possibly identical to Abishai of 2 Sam 23:18. Other bearers include Levites in the Kohathite genealogy (1 Chr 6:25, 35), a priest who blew the trumpet before the Ark (1 Chr 15:24), and a Levite in Hezekiah's reform (2 Chr 29:12). The name likely derives from the root 'amas' meaning 'to carry, bear a burden.'

senses.1: Personal name of multiple Israelites spanning warrior, Levitical, and priestly roles. The most memorable bearer is the Davidic warrior of 1 Chr 12:19 whose Spirit-empowered pledge of loyalty echoes covenant language. Spanish and English consistently transliterate 'Amasai,' while French and German retain the Hebrew form in brackets, reflecting its less common appearance in those traditions.

gloss_terse: Anathothite — gentilicof Anathoth, designating a person from that Benjamite town
gloss_readable: A gentilic adjective identifying someone as a native of Anathoth, the Benjamite town about three miles northeast of Jerusalem. The designation is applied to warriors in David's elite guard — Abiezer (2 Sam 23:27; 1 Chr 11:28; 27:12) and Jehu (1 Chr 12:3) — and to Jeremiah himself in the mocking address of Jer 29:27. The article regularly precedes it: 'the Anathothite.' Spanish 'el anatotita' and German 'der Anathothite' both reproduce this articulated gentilic pattern.

senses.1: Gentilic adjective meaning 'the one from Anathoth,' applied to warriors in David's ranks (Abiezer, Jehu) and used as a geographic label for Jeremiah's hometown identification in Jer 29:27. The consistent article across languages — English 'the Anathothite,' Spanish 'el anatotita,' German 'der Anathothite' — underscores its function as a fixed epithet rather than a casual descriptor.

gloss_terse: sweet wine, fresh-pressed juice — newly extracted grape or fruit juice
gloss_readable: Denotes fresh-pressed, sweet juice — wine in its earliest, most potent stage before full fermentation. The prophets use it to paint vivid pictures: mountains dripping with it in the messianic age (Joel 3:18; Amos 9:13), and Israel's enemies forced to drink their own blood 'like sweet wine' (Isa 49:26). In Song 8:2, it appears as 'juice of my pomegranate,' extending the term beyond grapes. Joel 1:5 mourns its loss as a sign of devastating judgment.

senses.1: Fresh-pressed, sweet juice of grapes or fruit, representing abundance and unprocessed vitality. Used in eschatological visions of overflowing fertility (Joel 3:18; Amos 9:13) and in Song 8:2 as pomegranate juice in an intimate setting. Spanish 'mosto' (must, new wine) and French 'jus' (juice) highlight the freshly-pressed quality, while German 'Suesswein' (sweet wine) emphasizes the sweetness that distinguishes it from aged wine.

gloss_terse: tumors, hemorrhoids — swellings afflicting the Philistines as divine plague
gloss_readable: Refers to painful swellings or hemorrhoids inflicted as a divine plague. The word appears only in the narrative of the Ark's captivity among the Philistines (1 Sam 5–6) and in the covenant curses of Deut 28:27. The Masoretic Ketiv reads 'ofalim' while the Qere substitutes the euphemistic 'tehorim,' reflecting scribal sensitivity about the affliction. The Philistines' golden replicas of these tumors (1 Sam 6:4–5) as a guilt offering underscore the bodily and theological gravity of the plague.

senses.1: Bodily swellings or hemorrhoids sent as divine judgment, appearing in the Philistine plague narrative (1 Sam 5:6–12; 6:4–5) and Deuteronomic curses (Deut 28:27). The Ketiv/Qere variation reveals scribal discomfort with the term. Translations uniformly render 'tumors' — English, Spanish 'tumores,' French and German likewise — reflecting the medical understanding that these were painful, visible growths afflicting the Philistine populace.

gloss_terse: Ophel — the fortified mound or hill-spur within Jerusalem (and Samaria)
gloss_readable: Designates a fortified mound or hill-acropolis, used almost exclusively for the southern spur of Jerusalem's eastern hill. Micah 4:8 addresses it as 'tower of the flock, Ophel of daughter Zion,' linking it to royal authority. Nehemiah records repairs to the Ophel wall (Neh 3:26–27), while Chronicles notes fortification projects by Jotham and Manasseh (2 Chr 27:3; 33:14). In 2 Kings 5:24, the term may refer to a similar citadel-mound in Samaria.

senses.1: A fortified mound or hill-spur serving as an acropolis, primarily the ridge on the southern end of Jerusalem's Temple Mount extending toward the City of David. Used in Nehemiah's wall-repair accounts (Neh 3:26–27; 11:21) and Chronicler's fortification notices (2 Chr 27:3; 33:14). Spanish 'el Ofel' and English 'the Ophel' treat it as a proper toponym, while French and German retain the Hebrew in brackets, reflecting its specialized architectural-geographic meaning.

gloss_terse: young deer, fawn — a young stag or hart, used in Song of Solomon's imagery
gloss_readable: A young male deer or fawn, appearing exclusively in the Song of Solomon as part of its rich pastoral imagery. The beloved is compared to a young stag leaping over hills (Song 2:9, 17; 8:14), while the woman's beauty is likened to twin fawns of a gazelle (Song 4:5; 7:3). The construct phrase 'ofer ha-ayyalim' (fawn of the deer) pairs with 'tsevi' (gazelle) throughout, creating a dual-image of grace and vitality.

senses.1: A young hart or fawn, used in Song of Solomon's erotic-pastoral poetry to evoke agility, beauty, and youthful vigor. The beloved leaps like a 'fawn of the deer' (Song 2:9, 17; 8:14), and twin fawns serve as a figure for the woman's form (Song 4:5; 7:3). Spanish 'cervatillo' (little deer), French 'faon,' and German 'junger Hirsch' (young stag) all preserve the sense of youthful grace central to the imagery.

gloss_terse: hurt, pain, sorrow — physical or emotional wound, injury, or grief
gloss_readable: Encompasses both physical pain and emotional anguish. In Job 9:28, the sufferer dreads all his 'pains,' while Psalm 147:3 celebrates God as the one who 'binds up their hurts.' Proverbs uses it twice with distinct nuances: winking causes 'hurt' to others (10:10), and sorrow of heart crushes the spirit (15:13). The most theologically charged occurrence is Psalm 16:4, where 'their sorrows shall multiply' describes those who pursue other gods — pain as the wages of idolatry.

senses.1: Physical or emotional pain, hurt, and sorrow arising from suffering, wrongdoing, or idolatry. In Job 9:28, it denotes the totality of bodily and existential anguish; in Ps 147:3, God heals these wounds. Prov 15:13 pairs 'pain of heart' against a glad heart. Spanish 'dolor' (pain/grief) and French 'travail' (suffering/labor) capture the dual physical-emotional range, while the German bracketed forms suggest translation difficulty — the word resists a single equivalent.

gloss_terse: to follow at the heel, supplant, deceive — to grasp the heel or overreach craftily
gloss_readable: A verb derived from 'aqev' (heel), spanning meanings from the literal grasping of a heel to figurative cunning and deceit. Its most famous use is Esau's bitter wordplay in Gen 27:36: 'Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me twice.' Hosea 12:3 recalls this same heel-grasping from the womb. In Jeremiah 9:4, the verb warns that every brother 'acts the Jacob' — deceives thoroughly. Job 37:4 uses a related sense of restraining or holding back, showing the root's range from physical gripping to moral treachery.

senses.1: To grasp at the heel, supplant, or overreach with cunning — encompassing both the literal birth-narrative act (Hos 12:3, recalling Gen 25:26) and the figurative sense of deceitful undermining (Gen 27:36; Jer 9:4). Spanish 'engaña' (deceives) and 'engañando' (deceiving) foreground the treachery dimension, while French 'Jacob' and German 'Jakob' preserve the etymological pun linking the verb to the patriarch's name. Job 37:4's usage ('he restrains them') shows extension from heel-grasping to holding back.
